entry.title: Bicep Reveal First Album in Five Years, Drop Three New Songs
entry.summary: Slug features contributions from Lauren Duffus, Eartheater, George Riley, Clark, and Sassy 009
entry.content:
Northern Irish DJ duo Bicep have revealed details of their first album in five years. Slug arrives January 29 via Ninja Tune. Last month, Bicep shared three singles from the LP—“Air,” “Lemonder,” and “Viper”—and they’ve dropped another triptych alongside today’s announcement: “Gas,” featuring Lauren Duffus and Soarr; “Ultra,” featuring Eartheater and Saskia; and “Equarium,” featuring Kehina. The songs come with music videos directed by Young Replicant, which together form a short film about pigeon fanciers. Watch below.

The title Slug was inspired, according to press materials, by “the stark contrast between the land slug most people immediately picture and the extraordinary colours, shapes and intricate forms of their underwater counterparts.” “For this album we really wanted to massively broaden what we do,” they added in an accompanying statement. “We wanted to make a much more varied album than our previous ones and push what people might expect BICEP to sound like.”

Slug will mark Bicep’s follow-up to 2021’s Isles. The album features additional contributions from Clark, George Riley, and Sassy 009, among others. Bicep have also lined up a pair of new 2027 live dates: one at New York’s Knockdown Center on March 21, and one at London’s Old Royal Naval College on July 31.

Revisit Ben Cardew’s review of Isles.

entry.title: Romain Gavras Is Bummed About Those AI Versions of “Storm”
entry.summary: “Part of me wanted to quit filmmaking, move back to Greece, and become an olive farmer”
entry.content:
Anyone who caught Yung Lean’s MTV VMAs performance of “Storm,” his short film with director Romain Gavras’ audiovisual project Gener8ion, is no stranger to the complex choreography that went into the project. Unfortunately, that hasn’t stopped a bevy of copycats from “recreating” the film with AI, subbing in Yung Lean and the video’s crew of young male dancers for dogs, babies, grandmothers, Elon Musk, Jeffrey Epstein, and even Hitler.

The trajectory appears to have left no one more disappointed than Gavras himself, who told Vulture that the AI copies “made me sad for all the people who put in so much work on our video.” Per Gavras, the budget on the original film was “very, very, very, very low,” and he worked for free. Dancers were selected through a two-month casting search, and rehearsed with choreographer Damien Jalet for three days; it took Gavras about 15 tries to nail the unbroken take, captured on 16-mm film.

“A trend like this can make even good work look lame,” Gavras added. “Part of me wanted to quit filmmaking, move back to Greece, and become an olive farmer.” Although Gavras emphasized that he never intended “Storm” as a commentary on AI, he felt like AI companies took the video’s elaborate practical effects as a sort of dare. “The tech people were like, ‘Oh yeah? AI could never?’ Then they started replicating it."

Gavras also noted he’s exploring legal avenues to stop the slop, but the logistics of suing the multitudes of anonymous users behind the recreations are hairy to say the least. He told Vulture a few AI companies reached out about licensing the film, but he declined: “There’s an economic model coming that we didn’t want to be a part of."

In fact, all the copies were part of what galvanized him to present the project live at the MTV VMAs, where “Storm” was nominated for four awards. Gavras saw an opportunity to show the world that AI still can’t replicate what’s so cool about “Storm.”

“They’re missing the swagger of Yung Lean,” Gavras said. “He looks like a dangerous baby. There’s something in the imperfection of humanity, and the interior life of someone who dances or even someone who just smokes a cigarette, that’s not quite there yet. But who the fuck knows what will happen in a year.”

entry.title: Did Drake Steal “Janice STFU”?
entry.summary: Songwriter Aviel Hirschfield claimed his reference track is a smoking gun. Now you can hear the audio that he says proves it
entry.content:
A lawsuit alleging Drake stole the chorus for “Janice STFU” took a turn overnight, when the reference track at the heart of the dispute leaked on X. The track was recorded by plaintiff Aviel Hirschfield, a Grammy-nominated songwriter who, like Drake, contributed to Beyoncé’s “Heated.” His hand in the Iceman hit, however, is up for debate: Despite clear similarities between the reference track and finished song, Drake’s team strongly denies anyone else was involved in writing “Janice STFU.” A legal representative for Hirschfield confirmed to Pitchfork that the leaked recording—which is public as an exhibit in the lawsuit—matches the one submitted as evidence. Complex was the first outlet to report on the leak.

Hirschfield claims he sent his vocal take—which introduces the prominent interpolation of Lykke Li’s “I Follow Rivers”—to production duo FnZ, as well as other Drake associates, in the hope of reaching the rapper. When the finished song came out, the lawsuit claims, “Avi was stunned to hear Drake perform word-for-word, note-for-note, beat-by-beat, the exact same chorus that he (Avi) had recorded and sent.” Hirschfield says he asked for a co-writer credit and retroactive publishing splits but was turned away. He claims his metadata will prove his work on the track pre-dates Drake’s.

Drake’s team said he has “no connection or knowledge” of Hirschfield, adding in a statement to Billboard, “Let us be absolutely clear: These allegations are categorically, unequivocally and completely denied. There is not one iota of truth to these accusations, and we reject every attempt to portray these claims as established facts.” Drake’s label, Universal Music Group, is also named as a defendant in the lawsuit. “Janice STFU,” which spent two weeks atop the Hot 100 this spring, is the rapper’s biggest hit in years.

The chorus in the leaked track begins around the 45-second mark.

entry.title: They Are Gutting a Body of Water’s Doug Dulgarian Diagnosed With Cancer
entry.summary: The band have canceled a forthcoming tour but are currently keeping December dates in New York and Philadelphia
entry.content:
They Are Gutting a Body of Water founder Doug Dulgarian has been diagnosed with cancer. He shared the news on Instagram, and confirmed that the Philadelphia shoegaze band has canceled their forthcoming North American tour as a result, save for three December shows: two in Brooklyn on December 9 and 10, and a hometown show on December 18. A GoFundMe to support Dulgarian and the band while he undergoes treatment was also launched today.

According to Dulgarian, he received his diagnosis on October 16, the same day the band put out their new mixtape Kool Faith / Loosies II, which featured a cadre of collaborators including Spirit of the Beehive, Hotline TNT, RXK Nephew, Horse Jumper of Love, and Greg Mendez. The band’s tour was set to kick off on October 29 in Baltimore.

“The fact that i got the diagnosis the same day we put out a massive compilation featuring as many friends as i could muster, well that symbolism that is not lost on me,” Dulgarian wrote. “I know I can be real corny sometimes but music and community has given me a purpose in my life that I didn’t have before I found it.”

Read Dulgarian’s full statement below.

damn. super bummed to have to talk about this. and super bummed to do this

I was diagnosed with cancer last Friday, same day we put out Kool Faith. crazy day, every possible emotion lmao

we obviously can’t do the tour, as I need to get this figured out. i have treatment in a couple weeks

I have a feeling it will all work out. been thru a lot of things in my crazy and (atp) relatively long existence and im no stranger to putting my best foot forward and facing some difficult shit

I wanna make this clear. im not seeking pity. i do not want to sway your emotions to feel bad for me. I just want to inform you. I genuinely believe this will work out just fine. there are many people with much worse problems and my life has been so infinitely blessed and privileged & I never lose sight of that

also I don’t think that kind of mindset is beneficial. if I start to believe that i deserve pity from others, I would feel bad for myself, & that’s the beginning of giving up

this ain’t the end of the world

we’re gonna keep the Philly & nyc dates on the schedule in hopes I’ll be able to do it

lifes so weird man. im a firm believer that everything happens for a reason. most of the time i don’t understand why at the time, but it always makes sense in the end. im sure this situation is no different

the fact that i got the diagnosis the same day we put out a massive compilation featuring as many friends as i could muster, well that symbolism that is not lost on me

I know I can be real corny sometimes but music and community has given me a purpose in my life that I didn’t have before I found it. you live one time and I haven’t got time to not mean everything I say, or to leave things unsaid

i love nothing more than making music and seeing my friends & it breaks my heart to cancel a tour

I hope what I can walk away with from this situation is gratitude for another experience. ive been blessed to experience a full spectrum of emotion in my life. very good, very bad, a whole lot in between

im scared and unsure of how this will all go. the prognosis seems to be pretty good. thats cool

love yall

I’ll keep ya posted

-doug

entry.title: Lambrini Girls Announce 2027 North American Tour
entry.summary: The British punk duo also shared two new songs, including one about "a sad little man who gets radicalised by the manosphere"
entry.content:
Lambrini Girls are bringing their forthcoming album No Refunds stateside next year. Phoebe Lunny and Selin Macieira have revealed a 2027 North American tour, set to kick off in March in Washington, D.C. and wrap up in Portland, Oregon in April. The new dates, which will feature support from Irish punk band Sprints, slot in between a UK and European run they announced in September. Check out a full list of stops below.

The duo paired the announcement with the release of two new songs: “The Basement,” written about “a sad little man who gets radicalised by the manosphere,” and “Spilt,” an acoustic track exploring alcohol dependency. (“It was exciting and challenging to do something that’s so different to the rest of the album and what we do in general,” Selin shared in a statement.) Listen to those below.

Both songs will appear on No Refunds alongside the previously released “Bang Bang Bang” and “Cult of Celebrity.” No Refunds drops January 15, 2027, just over two years after Lambrini Girls shared their 2025 debut Who Let The Dogs Out. Since then, the duo have seen their fair share of hardship: Maceira stopped touring temporarily in late 2025 after experiencing a manic episode, and Lunny dealt with a brain injury on Lambrini Girls’ first Australian tour. In turn, they’ve billed No Refunds as a heavier record then their debut, and said in press materials it will deal with themes including AI and genocide.

Read about Who Let The Dogs Out at No. 29 in The 30 Best Rock Albums of 2025.

entry.title: Rosalía to Perform at Latin Grammys 2026
entry.summary: Anitta, Silvana Estrada, Mon Laferte, and Daddy Yankee will also take the stage in Las Vegas
entry.content:
The Latin Recording Academy has unveiled a performer slate including Rosalía and Anitta for next month’s Latin Grammys. The two singers, who are taking victory laps behind their records Lux and Equilibrivm, are both competing for Album of the Year. Others taking the stage include Silvana Estrada, Mon Laferte, Jorge Drexler, and Daddy Yankee. Roselyn Sánchez will host the ceremony on November 12 at the MGM Grand Garden Arena in Las Vegas, airing from 8 p.m. Eastern on Univision.

Drexler and Rosalía are among a cohort of artists with seven nominations at this year’s show, all tied for second behind pack leader and songwriter supreme Edgar Barrera. The other performers announced in the first batch are Banda los Recoditos, Kany García, Juanes, Carín León, Vivir Quintana, Rawayana, Elena Rose, and Xavi.

entry.title: Levon Helm’s Daughter Countersues Levon Helm Studios
entry.summary: She claims her successor seized control of the iconic music venue through improper means
entry.content:
In August, Amy Helm—the daughter of late Band member Levon Helm, and a singer-songwriter in her own right—was sued in federal court for self-dealing, trademark infringement, and causing $2 million in damages to Levon Helm Studios (LHS), among other charges. Amy Helm has now countersued the studio, alleging that her successor, Brian Parillo, used invalid corporate actions to take control of the famed music venue in Woodstock, New York.

In May, Amy Helm was removed as president of LHS by her stepmother and Levon's widow, Sandra Helm, as well as LHS shareholders Parillo and Barbara O’Brien, over allegations of mismanagement. In response, Amy Helm accused Parillo of financial exploitation and elder abuse of Sandra Helm in a June court filing; Parillo denied those charges. There was also a physical dispute between Parillo and Amy Helm after her removal, during which police were called to LHS. No charges were filed.

In a new 34-page complaint filed on October 16 in New York Supreme Court, Amy Helm alleges that Parillo took control of LHS by way of voting assignments. Amy and Sandra Helm both own 40 percent of the company, while Parillo and O’Brien each own 10 percent. The lawsuit states that Parillo claimed voting assignments from Sandra Helm and O’Brien—thus receiving a purported 60 percent of the company’s power despite owning only 10 percent of its shares—and declared himself director, president, secretary, and treasurer of LHS. Amy Helm’s attorneys state she never signed any documents consenting to that change, that no shareholder meeting was held, and that his takeover is void.

The lawsuit also claims Parillo’s actions amount to “undue influence” over Sandra Helm, citing her sworn affirmation in a separate dispute over Levon Helm’s estate, in which her stepmother allegedly said, “I thought, ‘they’ve conned me.‘ I’m so gullible, they’re taking advantage of me. How do I undo this? I don’t know why I keep doing this.” Also cited in the lawsuit is a July order from Ulster County Surrogate’s Court appointing a guardian ad litem for Sandra Helm in the estate proceeding, in which she was described as “a person under disability” and directed the guardian to report on her ability to participate in the case.

Pitchfork has reached out to representatives for Amy Helm and Levon Helm Studios for comment.

Back in August, LHS claimed Amy Helm charged $400,000 to the studio to cover personal expenses, took an additional $200,000 from the Levon Helm Estate (including from an LLC that distributes royalties from Levon’s final albums, thus blocking the payment to those who worked on the records), and infringed on the Midnight Ramble name—a concert series her father hosted at LHS, which was continued under her leadership following his death—by creating her own trademark, Helm Family Midnight Ramble, and then diverting the revenue into her own company.

In an interview with the Overlook this summer, Sandra Helm responded to her stepdaughter’s early claims, stating, “I didn’t like that they wanted to portray Brian like some kind of a puppet master or Svengali that came in and overtook my mind. It’s been blown out of proportion. I just wanted to restructure Levon Helm Studios and bring it back to the glory days. And it’s as simple as that.”

entry.title: Muna Safe After Tour Bus Fire
entry.summary: Naomi McPherson is searching for “the grandchild of the warlock whose curse is wreaking havoc on my life”
entry.content:
The Gets So Hot Tour may have gotten a little too hot. Muna appeared on Los Angeles’ KTLA 5 local news network today after their tour bus caught fire in Burbank, California. The band have since confirmed that no one was injured, writing in an Instagram post, “many personal items were lost but we’re all safe, thank goodness ❤️‍🩹.”

In a comment under the post, Muna’s Naomi McPherson added, “if anyone could help me find the grandchild of the warlock whose curse is wreaking havoc on my life so that i can carry em up the mountain & fulfill the prophecy / undo the curse that has befallen me that would be much appreciated.” McPherson was absent from several of the band’s shows last month as they cared for their mother, who was suffering from terminal cancer.

As of writing, Muna’s Gets So Hot Tour will proceed as planned, with their next performance set for Wednesday, October 21 at Red Rocks.

Revisit Marissa Lorusso’s review of Muna’s new album Dancing on the Wall.

entry.title: Brooklyn Street Named After Late Baby’s All Right Co-Founder Billy Jones
entry.summary: “Billy did more for music in New York than what can be put into words”
entry.content:
Billy Jones, the late co-founder and owner of Baby’s All Right along with several other New York City nightlife staples, has a new street to his name. Billy Jones Way was unveiled during a ceremony on Sunday, on the corner of Bedford Avenue and Broadway in Brooklyn, just down the street from Baby’s. Jones died in 2025 from glioblastoma. He was 45.

“Billy did more for music in New York than what can be put into words. Every fresh-oﬀ-the-boat artist or music obsessive who was smart enough to send him a message, got a reply, a coﬀee, and, more often than not, something that felt like the beginning of a story,” said Baby’s owner Tom Moore during ceremony. “When Billy saw that blend of sound and vision, he cheered it on. He knew that this was the most basic principle of show business—that an audience made an idea into an act, and that an act could become part of the big story. Baby’s All Right is the house that his cheer built and where countless stories have started since.” 

In addition to Baby’s, Jones opened New York City venues including Night Club 101, Elvis Guesthouse, the Dance, and Funny Bar. Following the street unveiling, Baby’s All Right hosted a party featuring surprise sets from Blood Orange, Porches, Fcukers, and more.

entry.title: Watch Cardi B Blaze Through Her No-Brakes Tiny Desk Performance
entry.summary: The rapper’s backing band gave fresh, rock-inflected updates to singles like “ErrTime,” “Up,” and “Bodak Yellow”
entry.content:
Cardi B is probably as well-known for her banter as her bars, but she was (almost) all business during her new NPR Tiny Desk Concert. The rapper blazed through an eight-song set in 18 minutes, taking only brief pauses to shout out her backing musicians and, at one point, remark on the lack of Maryland crab cakes in her rider. Meanwhile, the nine-piece band gave fresh, rock-inflected updates to singles like Am I the Drama?’s “ErrTime,” “Up,” and “Bodak Yellow.” Watch it go down below.

In February, Cardi B returned to the Saturday Night Live stage for her second stint as musical guest, in an episode hosted by Alexander Skarsgård. So far she’s followed up Am I the Drama?, her 2025 album, with a couple of one-off tracks: the summer jam “Ah Ha” and “Don’t Chart,” her contribution to the Grand Theft Auto VI soundtrack.

Read about Cardi B in The 25 Funniest Rappers of All Time.

entry.title: Hot Chip’s New Album Puts Them A Long Way From Kansas
entry.summary: Lead single “Random Violence” is a tribute to the late JD Twitch
entry.content:
Hot Chip have a new album on the way called A Long Way From Kansas, which is set to arrive on January 8. They paired the announcement with a new song, “Random Violence,” a tribute to the late Optimo DJ JD Twitch. Check out the Jack Cole-directed video of it below.

“Last year in September our old friend and brilliant DJ Keith McIvor of Optimo in Glasgow passed away after a diagnosis of an inoperable brain tumour a few months earlier,” Hot Chip’s Joe Goddard shared in a statement. "He largely inspired the words of the song. He was a passionate music lover and a staunch believer in socialism. Many of the words relate directly to his death and to memories of being in Sub Club in Glasgow where we met 20 years ago.”

A Long Way From Kansas marks bandmember Felix Martin’s first time singing on a Hot Chip record, and also features Beth Ditto and Eddie Chacon. The record follows Hot Chip’s 2022 album Freakout/Release. Since then, the band have shared a 2025 reissue of their greatest-hits collection Joy In Repetition, appeared on the second season of Netflix’s Beef, and celebrated the 20th anniversary of their second album, The Warning.

entry.title: Watch Taylor Swift Debut “The Fate of Ophelia” Live at the Academy Museum Gala
entry.summary: She also performed “Love Story,” “Blank Space,” and her Toy Story 5 original song “I Knew It, I Knew You”
entry.content:
Taylor Swift took the stage last night at the sixth annual Academy Museum Gala, a Los Angeles fundraising event benefitting the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures. The singer-songwriter gave her The Life of a Showgirl track “The Fate of Ophelia" a live debut, and also performed "Blank Space,” “Love Story,” and “I Knew It, I Knew You,” the original song she wrote for Toy Story 5. Watch videos from the night below.

Conan O’Brien, who voiced Toy Story 5’s potty training gadget Smarty Pants, introduced Swift’s performance: “She’s John, Paul, George and Ringo all in one,” he said. Swift’s set follows the release of The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore, an expanded edition of the 2025 album with four new tracks. She debuted the Dakota Johnson and Colin Farrell-starring music video for “Patient Zero” at the MTV Music Video Awards earlier this month, where she brought home the inaugural Artist Director Honors and Video of the Year for “The Fate of Ophelia.” The songs constitute the first new music she’s released since tying the knot with husband Travis Kelce at Madison Square Garden in July.

entry.title: John Wilson Is Making a Harry Styles Tour Documentary
entry.summary: The How to With John Wilson creator will direct a film about the star’s Together, Together tour
entry.content:
A Harry Styles tour documentary directed by John Wilson is on the way. Variety reports that The History of Concrete director and creator of HBO’s How to With John Wilson has been filming Styles’ 30-night residency at New York’s Madison Square Garden for a forthcoming project produced by Universal Pictures Content Group, Peanut World Pictures, and Styles.

Styles’ current MSG run kicked off in August and concludes at the end of this month; it’s the longest single-engagement residency the venue has ever hosted. Although the film will be Wilson’s first artist documentary, he has worked in music before. Last year, he directed the music video for Bon Iver’s “Everything Is Peaceful Love,” which appeared on the singer-songwriter’s album SABLE, fABLE.

Revisit our review of Kiss All the Time. Disco, Occasionally.

entry.title: A$AP Rocky Recruits Jeremih and Reggie for “Shroom Clouds”
entry.summary: Teased since 2021, the song launches Don’t Be Dumb - Disc 2
entry.content:
A$AP Rocky has finally dropped “Shroom Clouds,” a song he performed a handful of times in 2021 and ’22 before putting it on the backburner. Now completed with guests Reggie and Jeremih, the song is out via A$AP Worldwide/RCA, along with a technicolor video directed by Rocky, Aisultan Seitov, and Pietro Biz Biasia.

Produced by Sleeping Bear and Hector Delgado, “Shroom Clouds”—previously titled “Mushroom Clouds”—is the first taste of Don’t Be Dumb - Disc 2, Rocky told Billboard. (That detail is unconfirmed in the single’s press release.) “Disc 2 is all of the songs that I dropped that those alter egos didn’t get an album to live on, because the next chapter is right after that,” he elaborated. Rocky is currently preparing to tour Australasia.

Correction: An earlier version of this story was published with a photo of Travis Scott, due to a mistaken label on Getty Images.

entry.summary: Stream new releases from Fontaines D.C., the Avalanches, @, and more
entry.content:
With so much good music being released all the time, it can be hard to determine what to listen to first. Every week, Pitchfork offers a run-down of significant new drops available on streaming services. This week’s batch includes new albums from Fontaines D.C., the Avalanches, @, and more. Subscribe to Pitchfork’s New Music Friday newsletter to get our recommendations in your inbox every week. (All releases featured here are independently selected by our editors. When you buy something through our affiliate links, however, Pitchfork earns an affiliate commission.)

Fontaines D.C.: Dopamine Chamber [XL]

Fontaines D.C. continue their evolution from underground rock insurgents to arena-baiting anthem merchants on their Romance follow-up. Lead single “Marianne” infuses sleazy synth-pop with the air of a haunted lullaby, while—in a pairing that makes more sense than it should—the Irish band unites with fellow crossover sensation Rosalía on “Where Is Gone?” The psychedelic blurring of genre boundaries plays off the titular concept, which, says Grian Chatten in press materials, describes the environment of the album itself. “You step inside and we test these different mind- or mood-altering pieces of music on you.”

@: Autosmile [4AD]

Titled after a Twitter meme, Autosmile by @ plays out like a series of private jokes told between friends. Those friends—Filipczak and Victoria Rose—got their start as folk-pop pranksters, but on their 4AD debut, they’ve leveled up into a brain-rotted Rawlings and Welch. Before Autosmile, you’d never hear Rose sing a lyric as nakedly sincere as “I don’t know how I belong to you, but I do somehow.” For the first time, the band with the most un-Googleable name in showbiz sounds marginally legible.

The Avalanches: No Bad Memories [Modular]

Those of us over a certain age all have that one jingle—a corporate ditty imprinted in our memory like a painting at Lascaux. (Mine? Education Connection. My Gen X mom’s? The original Big Mac theme.) Leave it to the Avalanches, masters of making up for lost time, to run with this phenomenon. The duo’s first proper LP since the pandemic draws inspiration from lost jingles and now-defunct technology like those two buddies pictured above. The features across the 31-song project bring a similar “old becomes new again” spirit to the group’s anhedonia-flecked electronica, uniting legends such as Yellow Magic Orchestra cofounder Haruomi Hosono with fresher-faced experimentalists Portraits of Tracy. Who knew hauntology could be so fun?

Rachel Chinouriri: I Think I Spoke Too Soon [Parlophone]

On the follow-up to her 2024 debut, What a Devastating Turn of Events, Rachel Chinouriri makes a home in the mirror-polished smear between Y2K pop and the slick UK indie that surfaced in its wake. She previewed the LP with the synth-pop sugar rush “One Song Away From Crying” and its darker counterpart “Make Believe,” which is about “allowing someone who clearly hates me to have access to me at any moment,” she wrote in a statement. Recent tour support slots with Gracie Abrams and Florence + The Machine hint at where the Londoner has her compass set.

Sophia Stel: The Greatest Album of All Time [A24]

The Greatest Album of All Time, Sophia Stel’s first album for A24’s nascent label, is an appropriately cinematic survey of life during an ascendant career moment: bigger crowds, new hangers-on, and long stretches on the road far from home. To hold on to some semblance of consistency, the Canadian singer-songwriter-producer kept her set-up similar to the DIY home studio where she made her 2025 EP, How to Win at Solitaire. Still, these moody and reflective dance-pop cuts constitute a big level up: a reminder that great pop gets down to a science, and properly wielded Autotune is an art form in itself.

Jacques Greene: JG [LuckyMe]

In my mind, Montreal producer Jacques Greene has always been an after-hours producer, someone whose reflective, R&B-inflected dance music befits a cozy living room at 5 a.m. more than an actual dancefloor. With the first bass drop of JG, listeners will immediately sense this album is different. On his first solo LP in seven years, Greene’s crystalline melodies and poppy vocals find a perfect marriage with 2-step, dubstep, and deep, deep basslines.

They Are Gutting a Body of Water: Kool Faith / Loosies II [ATO/Julia’s War]

They Are Gutting a Body of Water’s Doug Dulgarian still has fond memories of the jewel-cased mixtapes he’d pick up on the cheap as a kid, and the expansive yet hyper-regional feel of a genre-spanning track list spliced together by a local radio DJ. TAGABOW’s new mixtape gives the Philly band their very own DJ moment, compiling cuts with an array of Julia’s War labelmates and friends-of including Spirit of the Beehive, Greg Mendez, Hotline TNT, DJ Manny, Lucy (Cooper B. Handy), and RXKNephew. “The word mixtape initially meant a homespun tape that you typically listened to yourself or gave to somebody else,” Dulgarian explained in press materials. “For me who was born later, it meant mashups of all my favorite artists by local DJs. And so that’s what I did with this one, mashups of all my favorite artists.”

Dummy: Do You Love the Color of the Sky? [Polyvinyl]

Although Dummy joke that “making music shouldn’t be fun” in press materials for their new album, the Los Angeles quintet suffuses easy jubilance into Do You Love the Color of the Sky? Newly incorporating breakbeats into their bread and butter of ambient shoegaze and chamber-leaning electronic pop, the band tackles thorny social topics like the surveillance state and government overreach, carefully guided by vocalist Emma Maatman’s unmistakeable lilt.

Worldpeace DMT: Stick Around for Tea [WPDMT]

In a flush year for the nascent field of “laptop twee,” Britain’s Worldpeace DMT have stood out for their sharp but sincere bricolage of mid-2000s indie, jangly vintage pop, and appropriately tongue-in-cheek New York downtown worship. Leo Fincham and Rowan Miles (who splits time between this band and her more post-hyperpop-minded duo the Femcels) keep the momentum up on the charming Stick Around for Tea. Following in the ersatz footsteps of Belle & Sebastian and their Pacific Northwest brethren at K Records, they’ve filled out their sound with more layers and lusher production without sanding down the peculiarities that make them great.

Geologist and Kyle Simon: The Sirens [Outside Time]

The origin story behind The Sirens sounds like the wishful thinking of a sci-fi obsessive-turned-conspiracist. Animal Collective’s Geologist conceived the album at the Joshua Tree observatory of visual artist Kyle Simon, harnessing the power of the moon to record music. Simon rotated a telescope towards the night sky while photodiodes detected light from planets and stars—which was then converted into an electrical signal with an analog amplifier. Geologist ran it through his modular synth rig as control voltage; by shifting pitch, filter, and rhythm, he listened to nature in real time as if he was actively among the stars. Eat your heart out, Muse.

Listen on Apple Music

Heavens to Betsy: Baby’s Gone [Kill Rock Stars]

Heavens to Betsy—the pre-Sleater-Kinney duo of Corin Tucker and the Husbands’ Tracy Sawyer—haven’t released an album since 1994, but their comeback LP, Baby’s Gone, has been even longer in the making. The record brings together 16 tracks from multiple releases: a long-lost demo the pair recorded in 1992, the following year’s These Monsters Are Real, and 1994’s Direction 7” recordings. Older and wiser but as full of conviction as they were all those decades ago, Heavens to Betsy remind us that righteous feminist fury never loses its relevance or power.

entry.title: Lana Del Rey Joins Zach Bryan on New Song “Lies”
entry.summary: Bryan’s new EP Young Manhood and Other Donatable Organs—which he’ll support with a 2027 tour—is out now
entry.content:
Over two years after Lana Del Rey formally announced her eighth album, she’s still cooking up Stove and the “companion record” she teased in July. But after delivering “White Feather Hawk Tail Deer Hunter” in February, she’s reappeared as a featured artist on Zach Bryan’s new song “Lies.” Check out the duo’s collaboration below.

“Lies” appears on Bryan’s freshly released EP Young Manhood and Other Donatable Organs, which has a song with Turnpike Troubadors and backing vocals from Katy Kirby. The drop follows the January arrival of his 25-song fourth album With Heaven on Top, which also came with an acoustic version. That record followed 2024’s The Great American Bar Scene, and a 2023 solo, self-titled LP.

Earlier this week, Bryan announced plans for a 2027 tour across North America and Australia. The run kicks off in April in Minneapolis, and will alternate opening acts from a roster including Vance Joy, Emma Ogier, Gabriella Rose, and others. Creedence Clearwater Revival’s John Foggerty will also appear as a “special guest.” Bryan has spent a good portion of 2026 on the road, touring with support from Dijon, MJ Lenderman, Alabama Shakes, Kings of Leon, Gregory Alan Isakov, and more.

Read why we ranked Zach Bryan’s “Pink Skies” at No. 79 in The 100 Best Songs of 2024.
